faq.a: The parasite deposits hemozoin pigment and creates vacuoles that stain basophilic, indicating intracellular infection.
faq.q: Why does a malaria‑infected red cell look different under the microscope?

faq.a: It can show cytopathic changes (e.g., nuclear enlargement) but specific viral antigens need immunohistochemistry.
faq.q: Can a routine H&E stain detect viral infections?

faq.a: RER dilation with eosinophilic inclusions indicates protein synthesis stress from hepatotoxic drugs.
faq.q: What organelle change suggests drug‑induced liver injury?

exam: A 35‑year‑old with fever and jaundice from a rural clinic has a liver biopsy showing swollen mitochondria – what is the most likely pathophysiological mechanism? — Impaired oxidative phosphorylation leading to cellular hypoxia; consider sepsis or antimalarial toxicity.

You see eosinophilic RER expansion in a kidney biopsy of a patient with HIV – which disease process does this support? — HIV‑associated nephropathy with protein overload; differentiate from diabetic nephropathy by lack of basement‑membrane thickening.

A patient with chronic cough from a TB‑endemic area has granulomas with caseation; what organelle injury underlies the necrosis? — Lysosomal rupture releasing hydrolytic enzymes causing tissue breakdown.
In a malaria‑endemic region, a peripheral smear shows pigment‑laden macrophages; how does this guide treatment? — Confirms recent Plasmodium infection; start artemisinin‑based therapy promptly.

A child with sickle‑cell disease presents with acute chest syndrome; biopsy shows mitochondrial swelling – what does this indicate for prognosis? — Mitochondrial dysfunction predicts severe hypoxia and higher mortality; aggressive supportive care needed.
When electron microscopy is unavailable, which stain can help identify fungal infection in tissue? — PAS stain; positive result indicates polysaccharide‑rich fungal cell walls.

A patient on antiretroviral therapy develops hepatic RER dilation; which drug class is most likely responsible and why avoid it? — Nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors cause mitochondrial toxicity; avoid due to risk of lactic acidosis.

How would you differentiate drug‑induced liver injury from viral hepatitis on histology? — Drug injury shows RER swelling and eosinophilic bodies; viral hepatitis shows ballooning hepatocytes with ground‑glass nuclei.
ai.title: Cell Organelles Histology
ai.subject: Anatomy
ai.summary: Cell organelles are the functional subunits of eukaryotic cells. Understanding their microscopic appearance helps clinicians interpret tissue biopsies and recognize disease‑related changes, especially when advanced imaging is unavailable.

b: Endoplasmic reticulum – protein (RER) or lipid (SER) synthesis
Golgi apparatus – protein modification and sorting
sections.p: Eukaryotic cells contain membrane‑bound organelles that perform specialised tasks. Histological stains (e.g., H&E, PAS, immunohistochemistry) reveal their size, shape and content, guiding diagnosis of infections, malignancies and metabolic disorders.

b: Nucleus: large, basophilic with prominent nucleolus
Golgi: stacked pink‑purple cisternae near nucleus
sections.p: Organelles are distributed throughout the cytoplasm; their density varies with cell type (e.g., hepatocytes have abundant SER, lymphocytes have prominent nuclei). Light microscopy shows size and staining patterns; electron microscopy is required for detailed morphology.
Organelles interact closely: mitochondria cluster near SER for lipid metabolism; Golgi receives proteins from RER; lysosomes fuse with autophagosomes to recycle organelle components.

b: Capillary perfusion essential for ATP generation
sections.p: Organelles depend on cellular oxygen and nutrients delivered by capillary networks. In low‑resource settings, hypoxia from severe anemia or malaria can impair mitochondrial function, visible as cytoplasmic vacuolisation on biopsy.
Nerve impulses do not directly innervate organelles, but neuro‑hormonal signals regulate mitochondrial biogenesis and lysosomal activity via second‑messenger pathways.

b: Energy production → organ failure when impaired
Protein folding → ER stress in infections
sections.p: Each organelle contributes to cell survival: nuclei store genetic information; mitochondria generate energy; ER synthesises proteins and lipids; Golgi packages secretions; lysosomes degrade waste; peroxisomes detoxify reactive species.

b: RER dilation → viral hepatitis, protein overload
Lysosomal rupture → tissue necrosis in TB
sections.p: Altered organelle morphology signals disease. In malaria, parasitized erythrocytes show pigment‑laden vacuoles. HIV‑associated nephropathy displays podocyte foot‑process effacement with mitochondrial swelling. Tuberculosis granulomas reveal caseating necrosis with lysosomal rupture.

t.b: What structural changes are present? – Identifies organelle injury patterns that narrow differential diagnosis
Does the cell contain glycogen or mucopolysaccharide? – Positive PAS suggests fungal infection or storage disease
Is a viral protein present? – Positive result confirms viral cytopathic effect when electron microscopy unavailable

b: Link pigment‑laden macrophages to recent malaria exposure
Correlate granulomatous inflammation with TB risk factors
Recognise lysosomal overload in chronic hepatitis B
sections.p: Examiners test ability to link microscopic findings to bedside clues. Remember common tropical patterns: malaria pigment in macrophages, TB caseation, sickle‑cell induced mitochondrial dysfunction.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe sepsis with organ failure (mitochondrial dysfunction)
Acute hepatic failure with massive RER dilation
Rapidly progressive renal failure with lysosomal rupture
